It started a little over a year ago. I’ve been flying commercial jets for decades, so I’m used to medicals and the odd scraped knuckle in the cockpit. But after an incident on a layover—I’d rather not get into all the details, it involved a pretty bad injury—I just haven’t been the same around anything medical or bloody.

Now even walking past a clinic in the airport or seeing a needle on TV makes my chest tighten. If I have to get blood drawn for my flight physical, I’ll start sweating in the waiting room, my heart’s pounding, hands shaking, and I feel like I can’t quite catch my breath. A couple of times I thought I might pass out, so I avoid looking at the equipment or the nurse’s hands. My wife says I look pale and clammy.

I don’t have any problems actually flying, but I do catch myself worrying ahead of time about the next medical exam or if someone might get hurt on board. I try to push it out of my mind, but the physical reaction feels almost automatic when anything medical comes up.
D012-D018_h001.question_a:
It’s a little embarrassing, given what I do for a living, but I have this huge problem with anything medical—especially blood and needles. Flying a 777 full of people doesn’t faze me, but if I even see a needle on TV, I feel my chest tighten, my heart starts pounding, my palms get sweaty, and I feel lightheaded, like I might pass out.

This really ramped up after an incident about two years ago. We had a passenger with a bad hemorrhage mid‑flight. There was a lot of blood in the cabin while the crew and a doctor on board tried to stabilize him. I stayed focused in the cockpit, but afterward, I noticed that any time I’m near blood or think about injections, I get that same panicky reaction—short of breath, shaky, sometimes I have to sit down.

I don’t have nightmares about that flight, no flashbacks, no avoiding flying or airports. It’s specifically hospitals, blood draws, vaccines—anything like that. I’ll delay checkups, and when I can’t avoid them, I’m extremely anxious for days beforehand, worrying I’ll black out when they put a needle in me.
D012-D018_h001.question_b:
It started after that crash landing two years ago. We hit severe turbulence on approach, lost an engine, and for a few minutes I was sure we were all going to die. Nobody did, but a lot of passengers were badly hurt. I still see the blood in the cabin when I close my eyes.

Since then, anything medical sets me off. If I have to get blood drawn, or my wife turns on a hospital show, my heart takes off, my hands shake, I start sweating, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. I sometimes have to leave the room during the preflight safety briefing videos if they show injuries.

But it’s not just that. I’m having nightmares about the incident several times a week—waking up drenched, hearing the alarms in my head. I get flashbacks in the cockpit if we hit turbulence; for a moment I’m back in that descent. I avoid talking about that flight, avoid flying over that same route if I can. I’m always on edge, jumpy at sudden noises, and I can’t seem to relax, even at home. This has been going on pretty much continuously since the accident.

    D. Specific Phobia

I don’t like talking about the details, but since then I’ve been having a lot of trouble with certain places, especially tunnels and those long, enclosed hallways in hotels and parking garages. Elevators, too. I used to run around venues all day without thinking, and now I’ll do almost anything to avoid those areas.

If I have to go through one—like for a site visit with a couple—it’s like my body just reacts on its own. My chest tightens, my heart starts pounding, my hands get sweaty, and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. Sometimes my vision kind of narrows and I just want to turn around and get out of there immediately. It happens right away, the second I see the space or step inside.

I’m still working, but I’m rearranging floor plans, sending assistants instead of going myself, or choosing venues that don’t have those features. My husband says I seem “on edge” when we’re in parking structures or driving through tunnels, and he’s right—I’m constantly bracing for something bad to happen, even though I know it doesn’t really make sense.
D012-D018_h002.question_a:
It started about a year ago, after a car I was riding in got stuck halfway through a long tunnel because of an accident up ahead. We were trapped there maybe 40 minutes. Nothing terrible actually happened to me, but the whole time I felt like I couldn’t get out, like the ceiling was closing in.

Since then, anything like that sets me off—tunnels, parking garages, sometimes even long stretches under overpasses. As soon as I realize I have to go through one, my heart just slams in my chest, my hands sweat, I feel short of breath, like I’m going to lose control or faint, and all I can think is, “I have to get out of here.” I’ll beg my husband to take another route, even if it adds an hour, or I’ll turn down venue visits if they require going through a tunnel.

Outside of that, I’m okay. I don’t have nightmares about the incident, no flashbacks, and I’m not jumpy in general. It’s really just that kind of enclosed driving situation that triggers this intense, immediate panic.

It kicks in immediately, before I even have time to think it through.

It’s not just the fear, though. I keep having flashes of the accident—at night, in the shower, even during ceremonies. I jolt awake from nightmares about falling off bridges. I’m jumpy with loud noises, exhausted from poor sleep, and I avoid any venue that requires crossing a bridge, which is starting to affect my work and my marriage.

If I even see a dog across the street, my heart races, my hands sweat, and I feel like I can’t breathe. I’ll cross the road, turn around, whatever it takes to avoid them. The worst part is the worrying beforehand: if my wife suggests a walk in the park or visiting our daughter—she’s got a small dog—I start getting anxious just imagining a dog coming near me. I sometimes go anyway for family events, but I’m tense the whole time, on edge, watching the dog’s every move and just waiting to leave.

I don’t really have nightmares about the attack, and I’m not reliving it over and over. It’s mainly this intense, specific fear around dogs that hasn’t let up for years.

I’ll keep checking the weather app over and over at my desk instead of focusing on files.

I can’t always avoid it—sometimes I still have to drive home in it, or sit by the window at work during a downpour—and when I do, I’m just gripping the steering wheel or the armrest, trying to hide how panicked I feel. My coworkers probably just think I’m quiet, but inside I’m thinking about that night with the flooding and how powerless I felt.

D012-D018_h012.question_b:
